description: Firewatch Analytics is a two-person team from Sydney. We’re harmonising 20+ years of NASA MODIS and VIIRS fire hotspot data into an interactive burning activity calendar. You pick any area to see its fire seasons, record years and how this month compares with the norm.
summary:
Firewatch Analytics is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area of Australia.

Satellite fire records are split across sensors. MODIS (1 km pixels, since 2000) misses small fires that VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) detects, so joining them naively makes fire activity appear to jump about four-fold in 2012. We harmonise MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20 region by region, calibrating each 1° tile on the 2012–2025 overlap, to produce one continuous monthly record from 2000 to today. Tested on years it never saw, it explains 95% of the variation in monthly tile counts and removes the 2012 break (×4.33 down to ×0.93).

Users draw an area, type a point or upload a park boundary, then see when it usually burns, which years and months were extreme, and how today compares. A status line uses the last 7 days of live NASA data to show whether activity is normal or elevated, and names the area's critical fire period.

This gives emergency responders, scientists and land managers a consistent, trustworthy view of fire history and current conditions, with every number downloadable.
details:
Firewatch Analytics

What it does

Firewatch Analytics harmonises NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots from MODIS (Terra/Aqua, Collection 6.1, 2000–), VIIRS S-NPP (2012–2026) and VIIRS NOAA-20 (2018–) into one consistent monthly time series for every 0.1° cell across Australia, from November 2000 to today. A web app turns this into a burning-activity calendar (years × months) for any area the user chooses.

How it works

  1. Clean and grid. 34.7 million FIRMS detections are filtered to presumed vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence, then counted per 0.1° cell per month for each sensor.
  2. Harmonise. MODIS detects about 4.6× fewer hotspots than VIIRS, and the gap varies by landscape: about 3.4× in the arid interior and about 6× in eastern forests with many small fires. We fit a MODIS→VIIRS ratio for every 1° tile over the 2012–2025 overlap, shrinking sparse tiles toward their regional value. NOAA-20 is calibrated to S-NPP, fills S-NPP outage months, and takes over after S-NPP ended.
  3. Validate. Leave-one-year-out tests (2013–2025) give R² = 0.95 for 1° tile-months and a 4% median error for national monthly totals, versus 78% without harmonisation. A seam test shows that the naive 2012 jump (×4.33, p = 0.001) disappears after harmonisation (×0.93, p = 0.75), and placebo years show no break. A trust map rates every tile, and pre-2012 months carry 90% uncertainty ranges.

Features

  • Choose any area: presets; draw a rectangle, polygon or circle; type a point and radius or a bounding box; or upload a GeoJSON boundary (park, property, district).
  • Burning-activity calendar of harmonised detections for any date range, switchable to each raw sensor or to the anomaly versus a typical month.
  • Early-warning status line: compares the last 7 days of live NASA FIRMS data with what is typical for this time of year (below normal / normal / elevated / very high), and names the area's critical fire period (the shortest run of months holding at least 70% of its fire) and whether it is in that period now.
  • Live map of fires detected in the last 7 days, served through a serverless proxy that keeps the FIRMS API key private.
  • Season outlook showing what history says about the coming months (clearly labelled as not a weather forecast), a this-month-versus-every-year comparison, a seasonal profile, annual totals with a Theil–Sen / Mann–Kendall trend, and a plain-English summary.
  • Downloads: monthly CSV, per-cell CSV, individual live hotspots, and any chart as PNG. Shareable links.
  • Method and validation page with the regional map and limitations.

Benefits and impact

  • Emergency and early-warning teams can see at a glance whether an area is burning more than usual right now and whether its critical period is coming.
  • Scientists get a validated long-term record in which the sensor of origin no longer matters.
  • Land managers can upload their own boundaries and take the numbers and charts straight into planning and reports.

For example, the app shows December 2019, the height of the Black Summer, at 143× a typical December on the NSW and Victorian coast.

Creativity

Instead of one national correction factor, the harmonisation adapts to each landscape and is open about its own uncertainty through a trust map and uncertainty ranges. The status line brings together more than two decades of fire history and this week's live detections in a single sentence.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time products (MODIS, VIIRS S-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21) via LANCE/ESDIS.
  • Pipeline: Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy.
  • Web: JavaScript, Vite, Leaflet, Leaflet.draw, D3.js; hosted on Vercel with one serverless function.
  • Code is open source under the MIT licence.

Factors we considered

  • Colour-blind-safe palettes (inferno, purple–orange)
  • Mobile layout
  • Static, low-cost hosting
  • Keeping the API key out of the browser
  • Honest limits: detections measure hot pixels, not burned area; near-real-time data has no vegetation flag; and the tool supports decisions but is not a life-safety warning system.

We built it for Australia, and the pipeline is designed to scale to global FIRMS data.
